parsed.explanation: The operative regime is mixed: a protective subnational layer (explicit gender-identity discrimination protections since 2018/2023, X licenses, sanctuary city for care, no facility ban, no state targeting) sits inside a hostile national framework that governs every visitor's first contact. The national passport regime voids nonbinary markers and records sex at birth, entry screening flags document/presentation discrepancies as potential fraud carrying a lifetime ineligibility finding, and foreign governments have issued travel advisories after detentions. State-level custody harms (conversion-style policies, forced labour, sexual abuse) are documented but apply only to those who enter custody. No criminalisation of gender identity exists in this state; the severity if outed is refused entry, detention, or fraud exposure — major, not catastrophic. The state's protective layer lifts the score above the parent average, but the shared entry regime is the traveller's unavoidable exposure, holding it in the Elevated band.

entry_documents.exposure: National passport policy restricts markers to sex at birth, voids X markers; foreign ministry cable instructs officers to refuse cases with document discrepancies and consider fraud findings; trans travellers report confiscated passports and stranding; allied governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Litigation against the passport policy is ongoing; existing X passports remain valid until expiration; legal-aid FAQ exists for travellers.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry screening is the traveller's first and universal exposure; the state's protective layer cannot operate at the border.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National custody: corrections bureau adopted conversion-style policies (hair cutting, hormone removal) for trans prisoners; immigration custody reported forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement, sexual abuse; bureau stopped reporting trans prisoner counts.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Not documented; some executive orders blocked in court.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Detention arising from entry screening would place the traveller in national custody; the state's sanctuary order does not shield against federal custody.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans access to federally funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; ~half of all state/provinces have some facility ban; 4 make it criminal.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This state/province has no facility ban; the largest city requires gender-neutral bathrooms in public buildings; no criminal statute here.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State facilities and most public accommodations are accessible; national facilities (airports, federal buildings) follow the hostile national rule.

care_services.exposure: National orders frame care for minors as 'mutilation'; hospitals subpoenaed for records of patients under 19; funding freezes threaten programmes.
care_services.protection: Gender-affirming surgery lawful; no adult care prohibition in state; mayor declared sanctuary city shielding care seekers from external enforcement; 2026 risk assessment places state in low-risk tier.
care_services.interaction: Travelling adults and minors can access care locally; sanctuary order deprioritises enforcement of outside restrictions.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'radically pro-transgender' violent groups for neutralisation; 'radical gender ideology' rhetoric in law-enforcement memoranda; executive orders criminalise teachers facilitating social transition.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: State commission interprets sex discrimination to cover gender identity, investigates complaints and awards remedies; state regulations bind.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Hostile national framing raises outing probability and severity; state-level enforcement machinery is protective.

minors_guardians.exposure: State/province-level birth-certificate changes require parental request under 18; national child-care bans in 27 states/provinces; proposed national insurance bar; national rules target social transition of minors.
minors_guardians.protection: No state ban on gender-affirming care for minors; city ordinances bar youth-serving organisations from discrimination; sanctuary city protects travelling families.
minors_guardians.interaction: A trans minor travelling with a guardian faces national entry screening but protective state care and education access.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No statewide hate-crime statute covering gender identity (struck down 2008, reinstatement never passed); 2020 legislative flag ban signals hostility from some officeholders.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Explicit discrimination protections, municipal ordinances; state human relations commission remedies; anti-LGBTQ bias crimes nationally punishable under national hate-crime statute.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Street violence is a documented national concern; state protections are partial without a state hate-crime provision.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Uncertain whether the upper chamber codifies protections; sports bills pending; no X marker on state birth certificates; national fraud finding may follow from document mismatch at entry.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Sanctuary city order; state commission remedies; courts challenge national orders; legal-aid FAQ.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: State protections are regulations and interpretation, not statute, so their durability is uncertain; national regime is the operative boundary stage.

anchor_checks.comparison: This case is materially safer than Vellandra's 0.35-A: no blanket entry-bar regime for trans visitors, no state facility ban, no criminalisation of gender identity here, and a functioning state protective layer. The shared national entry-screening friction is the only comparable exposure, but it is less severe than the Vellandran register which refuses every visitor routinely.

Similar to Kestrel Isles' 0.55-B: discretionary border screening and document mismatch can cause denied entry, humiliation, and disruption, but no criminal prosecution or imprisonment follows from being outed. The national regime adds severity above 0.55-B because of potential fraud findings and custodial harms, so the case sits somewhat above 0.55-B.

This case is below 0.75-C: Meridia's regime is benign border screening with an appeal tribunal and no custody harms. Here the national framework includes documented custody harms (conversion-style policies, forced labour, sexual abuse), a hostile national threat-framing that raises outing probability, and multiple facility bans in neighbouring states, so the score cannot reach 0.75 despite the state's protective layer.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller's operative exposure is fixed at the national border: passport marker restrictions, discrepancy screening, fraud consideration, and a hostile national threat-framing, all of which raise the probability of outing and the severity if outed. Once inside the state, the protective layer (explicit discrimination protections, X licenses, sanctuary city, no facility ban, no criminalisation) reduces the severity of daily exposure. However, if the traveller is detained or arrested, national custody policies apply — documented conversion-style practices, forced labour and sexual abuse — and the state's sanctuary order cannot shield against federal custody. The state's own exposure is minimal; the national regime is the dominant exposure. The result is a rating above the parent average but well below the 0.75 tier because the state's protections cannot offset the severity and frequency of the national entry and custody regime.
